questions.q: You are driving on a road marked with this yellow diamond. What does it tell you?
a: You are on a priority road — crossing traffic yields to you
Give way at the next crossing
questions.e: The yellow diamond (B1) marks a priority road: at the crossings ahead, the other traffic must give way to you — usually confirmed by shark's teeth on their side.

questions.q: At an unmarked equal intersection, a CYCLIST approaches from your right. Who goes first?
questions.e: Right-before-left applies to all drivers — and cyclists are drivers too. A cyclist from the right at an equal crossing has priority over you.

questions.q: What is the difference between this sign and the give-way triangle (B6)?
a: This one requires a complete stop, always
This one applies only at night
questions.e: B6 requires yielding — stopping only if traffic is coming. The stop sign (B7) requires a full stop every time, even on an empty road.

questions.q: You are leaving a roundabout and cross the cycle path that circles it. Shark's teeth are painted on YOUR exit lane. Who goes first?
a: You — you are leaving the roundabout
The cyclist on the circling path
questions.e: Shark's teeth on your lane mean you give way — here to the cyclists circling the roundabout. On many roundabouts in the built-up area, the cycle path has priority.

questions.q: A police car approaches with blue lights flashing but NO siren. Does it have special priority?
a: No — it needs both lights AND siren
questions.e: The special priority applies to emergency vehicles using blue lights AND the siren together. Lights alone give no formal priority — though staying alert is wise.

questions.q: At an equal T-junction with no signs, you drive on the through road. A car comes from a road joining on your right. Who goes first?
a: You — you are on the through road
questions.e: An unmarked T-junction is still an equal intersection: right-before-left applies, and the joining road on your right has priority. The 'through road feels bigger' instinct is the trap.

questions.q: A traffic light shows red, but a priority-road sign stands at the same crossing. What do you follow?
a: The sign — priority roads never stop
questions.e: Lights override signs — that is the order of authority. A working traffic light switches the signs off, effectively; you stop at red on any road.

questions.q: On the roundabout itself, a car wants to enter from an approach road with shark's teeth. You are already circling. Who goes first?
a: You — the markings tell entering traffic to yield
questions.e: The shark's teeth at the entries put the duty on entering traffic: whoever is already on the roundabout goes first.

questions.q: This red triangle shows an uneven road surface. What does it require of you?
a: Nothing by law — it warns you to prepare
questions.e: Warnings never command. It tells you a bump or rough patch is coming so you can ease off — the action is yours to judge.

questions.q: A red ring with the number 50. You are doing 65. Are you within the law?
a: No — the ring sets a hard maximum
questions.e: The red ring is a prohibition: driving faster than the number is forbidden. It holds until another sign or the end of its stretch changes it.

questions.q: What does this blue circle with a bicycle mean for you as a car driver?
a: Cyclists may not use this road
That path is compulsory for cyclists — keep your car off it
questions.e: For cyclists it is a command: use this path. For you it is the counterpart: that lane belongs to bikes — do not drive or park on it.

questions.q: What does the white P on a blue square tell you?
a: A place where parking is allowed
questions.e: Blue square = information. The P marks parkeergelegenheid — a place where you are allowed to park.

questions.q: In the Netherlands this sign is blue, not green as in some countries. What does it announce?
questions.e: The blue square with the twin-carriageway symbol announces the motorway. It informs — and with the road type, the motorway rules and limits apply.

questions.q: The centre of the road carries a solid line and a dashed line side by side. The DASHED one is nearest your lane. May you cross to overtake?
a: No — a solid line is present
Yes, when safe — you read the line on your side
questions.e: With a double centre line you obey the line nearest you: dashed on your side means you may cross when safe; the solid line binds the other direction.

questions.q: Which shape/colour combination COMMANDS you to do something?
questions.e: Blue circle = gebod, a command (must). Red triangle warns, red circle forbids, blue square informs. Classify by shape and colour before reading the symbol.

questions.q: A dashed white line runs along the centre of the road. What does it permit?
a: Crossing it when that is safe
questions.e: A dashed line may be crossed when safe — for example to overtake. Solid is closed, dashed is open.

questions.q: On a road outside the built-up area with no signs at all, what is the speed limit?
questions.e: No sign means the road type decides: outside the built-up area the default is 80 km/h.

questions.q: This blue square with a white car marks the road you are entering. What is the default limit here?
questions.e: This is the autoweg (expressway): default 100 km/h. It also bans slow traffic — bicycles, mopeds, tractors.

questions.q: Why do motorway speed signs often carry a small '06:00–19:00' plaque under the 100?
a: The road closes outside those hours
100 is the daytime limit; at night a higher signed limit may apply
questions.e: The plaque is the daytime rule in the wild: 100 between 06:00 and 19:00 everywhere, with 130 (or 120) returning at night only where signed.

questions.q: The motorway entry was signed 130. A lit matrix board above your lane now shows 90 in a red ring. What is your maximum?
a: 90 km/h — the matrix board is binding
questions.e: A number in a red ring on a matrix board is a real, enforceable limit — exactly as binding as a metal sign, and it overrides what was posted before.

questions.q: You pass this sign. What does it mean?
a: The 30 zone ends — the road-type default applies again
questions.e: The greyed, struck-through zone sign ends the zone. After it, the ladder takes over — inside the built-up area that means back to 50.

questions.q: You drive out of the erf past this end sign onto the street. Who goes first?
a: You — you are joining from the right
Everyone else — leaving an erf counts as leaving an exit
questions.e: Leaving an erf is legally leaving an exit: you give way to all traffic — cars, cyclists and pedestrians.

questions.q: Which is the correct default speed ladder for car drivers (town / outside / autoweg / motorway)?
questions.e: 50 inside the built-up area, 80 outside, 100 on the autoweg, 130 on the motorway — with the daytime-100 rule on top. This ladder answers every unsigned speed question.

questions.q: You tow a trailer with your car on the autoweg (signed 100). What is your maximum?
questions.e: A car towing a trailer or caravan may do at most 90. Your vehicle's own ceiling applies whenever it is lower than the road's — the lowest number wins.

questions.q: How long does this 50 limit stay in force?
a: Until another speed sign, an end sign, or the end of its stretch changes it
questions.e: A posted limit holds until something changes it — a new number, an end-of-limit sign, or the end of the zone or road it applies to. You never get to assume it lapsed.

questions.q: A cycle lane (fietsstrook) with a solid line and bicycle symbols is painted on your road. May you park on it?
a: No — never park or stop on a cycle lane
questions.e: A marked cycle lane belongs to the bikes: you may not park on it, and you may not stop on it.

questions.q: What does this sign — a moped above a bicycle in a blue circle — mark?
a: A shared path, compulsory for both bicycles and mopeds
questions.e: This is the combined fiets/bromfiets path, common outside the built-up area — 45 km/h mopeds legitimately ride there alongside bicycles.

questions.q: Must the rider of a blue-plate snorfiets wear a helmet?
questions.e: Since 2025 snorfiets riders must wear a helmet too. Bromfiets riders (yellow plate) always had to.

questions.q: A person with a white cane waits at the kerb, not at a zebra. What do you do?
a: Give way — a white cane must always be given way
Sound the horn to warn them
questions.e: A blind person signalling with a white cane must be given way, zebra or no zebra, always.

questions.q: Ahead of you, a truck at an intersection first swings out to the LEFT while indicating RIGHT. What is happening?
a: It needs room for a wide right turn — do not dive into the gap
questions.e: Trucks swing out before tight right turns. The gap that opens on its right is exactly where its trailer will sweep — stay out of it.

questions.q: A tram has stopped at a tram stop and passengers step off into the road to reach the pavement. What must you do?
a: Stop and let them reach the pavement
questions.e: Passengers boarding or leaving a tram must be given the chance to cross to the pavement — you stop and wait.

questions.q: You see this triangle with a bicycle. At the crossing 100 m later, shark's teeth are painted on the CYCLISTS' path. Who yields at that crossing?
a: The cyclists — the shark's teeth are on their side
questions.e: The triangle only warned you. Priority at the crossing itself is set by the markings there — shark's teeth on the cyclists' path put the duty on them. (Stay alert anyway.)

questions.q: Where is a truck's LARGEST blind spot?
questions.e: The whole right side is the killer zone — plus directly in front of the cab and directly behind. If you cannot see the driver in his mirror, he cannot see you.

questions.q: A driver refuses the police breath test. What is the consequence?
a: It is an offence, treated as seriously as failing
questions.e: Refusing the breath (or saliva) test is itself an offence, punished on par with a serious failed test.

questions.q: You drove for 15 years abroad and just received your first Dutch licence. Which alcohol limit applies to you?
a: 0.2 promille — the novice limit runs on the Dutch licence
questions.e: Novice means the first five years of THIS licence. Foreign experience does not count — the clock starts when the Dutch licence is issued.

questions.q: You feel exhausted on a long evening drive. What is the correct response?
questions.e: Fatigue impairs like alcohol, and the only accepted answer is: recognise it, stop, rest. Coffee, windows and music are the trap options.

questions.q: Which document proves the car is registered and to whom?
questions.e: The kentekenbewijs (registration certificate) ties the car to its registration. The rijbewijs is your driving licence; the APK is the periodic inspection.

questions.q: Your friend's car has valid insurance but the APK inspection expired last month. May you drive it to the garage for repairs?
a: Yes — you are fixing the problem
No — an expired APK keeps the car off the public road (except driving to a booked APK appointment)
questions.e: With an expired APK the car may not be on the public road. The single narrow exception is driving to a booked inspection appointment — and the fine lands on the driver.

questions.q: Your phone is mounted in a cradle and you start navigation with a voice command while driving. Offence?
a: Yes — any phone use is banned
No — mounted and hands-free is legal
questions.e: The offence is in the hand, not in the phone. Mounted in a cradle and operated hands-free, the same phone is legal.

questions.q: An adult passenger in your back seat refuses to wear the seatbelt. Who gets the fine?
a: You — the driver is always responsible
questions.e: Adults are responsible for their own belt. The driver answers for passengers under twelve — for them, the fine is yours.

questions.q: What is the legal definition of 'stopping' (stilstaan) as opposed to parking?
a: Briefly letting passengers in/out or loading — and no longer
questions.e: Stopping is the brief functional halt: passengers in or out, loading or unloading, no longer than that takes. Everything beyond it is parking — a different legal act.

questions.q: A solid yellow line is painted along the kerb. What does it mean?
questions.e: Solid yellow = no stopping; dashed yellow = no parking. The kerb paint mirrors the two signs: slash bans parking, X bans stopping.

questions.q: A dashed yellow line runs along the kerb. May you stop there briefly to unload?
a: Yes — it bans parking, not stopping
questions.e: Dashed yellow bans parking; a brief functional stop for loading or passengers remains allowed — the paint version of the E1 slash.

questions.q: May you park with two wheels on the pavement to leave more room for traffic?
a: No — parking on the pavement is forbidden
questions.e: The pavement belongs to pedestrians. Parking on it is forbidden — considerateness to cars does not override it.

questions.q: Why is parking forbidden within five metres BEFORE a zebra crossing?
a: To keep the zebra paint visible
So pedestrians stepping out are visible, not hidden behind your car
questions.e: A car parked just before the zebra hides the pedestrian until they are in front of your bumper. The five metres keep the sightline open.

questions.q: You drive with high beam at night. A car approaches in the oncoming lane. What must you do?
a: Keep high beam — you need the view
Dip your lights — never blind oncoming traffic
Flash twice, then keep them on
questions.e: High beam never against oncoming traffic, and never close behind another car. You switch down the moment your light can blind.

questions.q: When may you use FRONT fog lights?
a: In fog, snow or rain that seriously reduces visibility
Only together with the rear fog light
questions.e: Front fog lights are for seriously reduced visibility — fog, snowfall, heavy rain. The rear fog light has the stricter rule: only below 50 m.

questions.q: Your roof box load partly covers the number plate. Is that allowed?
a: Yes, if the load is secured
No — a load may never cover lights or the plate
questions.e: A load must be secured AND may never cover your lights or number plate; a protruding load must be marked.

questions.q: You pass a row of parked cars and see a driver sitting in one of them. What is the insight answer?
a: Slow down and keep a door's width of space — the door may open
Sound the horn as you pass
questions.e: Someone at the wheel means the door may open. You pass slower and a door's width away — reacting to what COULD happen, not what is happening.

questions.q: A bus has stopped at a bus stop ahead on your right. You can pass easily. What does the exam want you to do?
a: Pass at unchanged speed — it is only a bus
Ease off and watch the front of the bus for crossing pedestrians
Stop behind the bus and wait
questions.e: Passengers who just got off cross in front of the bus, hidden until the last step. Ease off and watch its nose — and if it signals to pull out, let it.
